notes.front: After one lesson, a learner's short-field take-offs are still inconsistent. What does the drill and practice method call for?
notes.back: A) Further practice, directed by the instructor toward an objective, since learning continues every time practice occurs
notes.explanation: Learners learn by practising and applying what they have been told and shown; the instructor provides the practice and directs it toward an objective.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Drill and Practice Method”, p. 5-22
notes.evidence: They learn by practicing and applying what they have been told and shown. Every time practice occurs, learning continues. Effective use of drill and practice revolves around what skill is being developed. The instructor provides opportunities for learners to practice and while directing the process toward an objective.
notes.choices:
A) Further practice, directed by the instructor toward an objective, since learning continues every time practice occurs
B) One more demonstration, then move on to the next manoeuvre
C) Assign reading on take-off performance instead of flying
D) Use a case study of a take-off accident
notes.choicesExplained: B: the mind rarely retains and applies new practices after one exposure. C: learners learn by practising and applying what they have been told and shown. D: a case study builds analysis, not the repetition this skill needs.

notes.front: How do instructional aids differ from training media?
notes.back: Instructional aids are not self-supporting: they support, supplement or reinforce what is taught. Training media are any physical means that communicates an instructional message.
notes.explanation: An aid only assists the instructor in the teaching-learning process; it does not carry the lesson on its own.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructional Aids and Training Technologies”, p. 5-23
notes.evidence: Instructional aids are devices that assist an instructor in the teaching-learning process. Instructional aids are not self-supporting; they support, supplement, or reinforce what is being taught. In contrast, training media are generally described as any physical means that communicates an instructional message to learners.

notes.front: Instructional aids help gain and hold learners' attention. What caution does the handbook attach to this?
notes.back: The aid should keep learner attention on the subject; it should not be a distracting gimmick.
notes.explanation: Combining audio and visual stimuli is particularly effective, since the two most important senses are involved.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Reasons for Use of Instructional Aids”, p. 5-23
notes.evidence: help gain and hold the attention of learners. Audio or visual aids can be very useful in supporting a topic, and the combination of both audio and visual stimuli is particularly effective since the two most important senses are involved. One caution—the instructional aid should keep learner attention on the subject; it should not be a distracting gimmick.

notes.front: By how much do studies say instructional aids increase learners' retention?
notes.back: Results vary greatly: from a modest 10 to 15 percent to as much as 80 percent.
notes.explanation: The figures come from numerous studies of how well aids serve retention, and their indications vary greatly.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Reasons for Use of Instructional Aids”, p. 5-23
notes.evidence: Numerous studies have attempted to determine how well instructional aids serve this purpose. Indications from the studies vary greatly—from modest results, which show a 10 to 15 percent increase in retention, to more optimistic results in which retention is increased by as much as 80 percent.

notes.front: A class includes learners from several countries, and aviation jargon keeps causing confusion. How does the handbook say instructional aids can help?
notes.back: A) By using terms on the aid chosen precisely, so they mean the same to learner and instructor
notes.explanation: Growing technical terminology and culturally diverse learners make it necessary for instructors to be precise in their choice of terminology.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Reasons for Use of Instructional Aids”, p. 5-24
notes.evidence: Good instructional aids also can help solve certain language barrier problems. Consider the continued expansion of technical terminology in everyday usage. This, coupled with culturally diverse backgrounds of today’s learners, makes it necessary for instructors to be precise in their choice of terminology.
notes.choices:
A) By using terms on the aid chosen precisely, so they mean the same to learner and instructor
B) By adding long written explanations to each aid
C) By avoiding aids until the language barrier is gone
D) By removing all words from the aids
notes.choicesExplained: D: the handbook asks for precise terms, not none. B: words on an aid should be kept to a minimum. C: the handbook says good aids can help solve language barrier problems.

notes.front: How do instructional aids help with the relationships between material objects and concepts?
notes.back: They present relationships visually, and relationships presented visually are often much easier to understand.
notes.explanation: Subsystems within a physical unit, for example, are relatively easy to relate to each other through schematics or diagrams.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Reasons for Use of Instructional Aids”, p. 5-24
notes.evidence: Another use for instructional aids is to clarify the relationships between material objects and concepts. When relationships are presented visually, they often are much easier to understand. For example, the subsystems within a physical unit are relatively easy to relate to each other through the use of schematics or diagrams.

notes.front: How do instructional aids help an instructor who is asked to teach more in less time?
notes.back: A recording, picture or diagram replaces many words, so the learner gains knowledge faster and more accurately, and time is saved.
notes.explanation: Instead of describing a sound, object or function at length, the instructor plays, shows or presents it.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Reasons for Use of Instructional Aids”, p. 5-24
notes.evidence: For example, instead of using many words to describe a sound, object, or function, the instructor plays a recording of the sound, shows a picture of the object, or presents a diagram of the function. Consequently, the learner gains knowledge faster and more accurately, and the instructor saves time in the process.

notes.front: At which moment in a lesson does the handbook suggest an instructional aid is most likely to be appropriate?
notes.back: B) When learners are puzzled by a verbal description of a complex fuel system
notes.explanation: Aids are often appropriate when a point is complex and hard to put into words, or when learners are puzzled by an explanation or description.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Guidelines for Use of Instructional Aids”, p. 5-24
notes.evidence: The aids should be concentrated on the key points. Aids are often appropriate when long segments of technical description are necessary, when a point is complex and difficult to put into words, when instructors find themselves forming visual images, or when learners are puzzled by an explanation or description.
notes.choices:
A) While telling the opening joke
B) When learners are puzzled by a verbal description of a complex fuel system
C) On every point, so that no idea goes without an aid
D) When introducing a new idea in the conclusion
notes.choicesExplained: A: aids should be concentrated on the key points of the lesson. C: aids should be concentrated on the key points, not spread over all of them. D: new ideas should not be introduced in the conclusion at all.

notes.front: What two advantages does the marker board offer?
notes.back: Material can be erased so the surface is used again and again, and it is an excellent medium for joint learner-instructor activity.
notes.explanation: Its versatility and effectiveness give it advantages for most types of instruction.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Marker Board”, p. 5-25
notes.evidence: Its versatility and effectiveness provide several advantages for most types of instruction. First, the material presented can be erased, allowing the surface to be used again and again; and second, the boards serve as an excellent medium for joint learner-instructor activity in the classroom.

notes.front: Why are pictures, drawings and photographs especially effective as supplemental print material?
notes.back: They provide common visual imagery for instructors and learners, and realistic details needed for visual recognition of important material.
notes.explanation: Instructor and learner are, in effect, looking at the same image of the subject.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Supplemental Print Material”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Pictures, drawings, and photographs are especially effective because they provide common visual imagery for both instructors and learners. In addition, they also provide realistic details necessary for visual recognition of important subject material.

notes.front: An independent instructor buys a syllabus with spaces for her endorsements and records, which also reminds her and the learner of regulatory training benchmarks coming up. What type of instructional aid is this?
notes.back: D) Enhanced training material
notes.explanation: The handbook says training syllabi represent enhanced training material, with provisions for endorsements, recordkeeping and reminders of approaching benchmarks.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Enhanced Training Materials”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Training syllabi represent enhanced training material and contain provisions for instructor endorsements and recordkeeping. Such syllabi not only present the course of training in a logical step-by-step, building block sequence, they contain provisions to remind both learners and instructors of critical regulatory training benchmarks which are approaching.
notes.choices:
A) Test preparation material
B) Supplemental print material
C) An interactive system
D) Enhanced training material
notes.choicesExplained: B: that covers pictures, charts, diagrams and the like, not syllabi with recordkeeping provisions. C: that is computer software responding to the user's choices. A: that is designed to help applicants prepare for FAA tests.

notes.front: When using projected material, what should the instructor do before and after the presentation?
notes.back: Before: set up equipment and lighting, preview it and give learners an overview. After: allow time for questions and summarise key points.
notes.explanation: The handbook says use of projected materials requires planning and practice.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Projected Material”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Use of projected materials requires planning and practice. The instructor should set up and adjust the equipment and lighting beforehand and then preview the presentation. During a classroom session, the instructor should provide learners with an overview of the presentation before showing it. After the presentation, the instructor should allow time for questions and a summary of key points.

notes.front: When an instructor uses video, the presentation {{c1::is not designed to replace the instructor}}.
notes.back: is not designed to replace the instructor
notes.explanation: Instructors should plan which points to stress and be available to summarise the presentation and answer questions.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Video”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: The presentation is not designed to replace the instructor. Prior planning will help determine the important points and concepts that should be stressed, either during the presentation or summary. Instructors should be available to summarize the presentation and answer any questions learners may have regarding content.

notes.front: What is the branching technique used in interactive systems?
notes.back: Programming questions or directions to offer several possible courses of action, so the user chooses how to move between sequences.
notes.explanation: A program that responds 'That was incorrect. Go back and try again' is using it.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Interactive Systems”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: The questions or directions are programmed using a branching technique, which provides several possible courses of action for the user to choose in order to move from one sequence to another. For example, a program may indicate, “That was incorrect. Go back to … and try again.”

notes.front: When CAL is used as an instructional aid, how does the instructor's role change?
notes.back: The instructor leaves centre stage and becomes a supportive facilitator, circulating among learners working alone or in small groups.
notes.explanation: Learners become more involved, and the instructor serves as a guide or resource expert.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Computer-Assisted Learning (CAL)”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: With CAL, the roles of both learner and instructor change. Learners become more involved and instructors may no longer occupy a center-stage position in a typical classroom setting. Instead, instructors become supportive facilitators. As such, they serve as guides or resource experts and circulate among learners who are working individually or in small groups.

notes.front: How does a mock-up differ from a cut-away?
notes.back: Mock-up: used instead of a real object too costly, dangerous or unobtainable. Cut-away: built in sections to reveal internal structure.
notes.explanation: A mock-up may also highlight components for learning and leave out nonessential elements.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Models, Mock-ups, and Cut-Aways”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: in place of the real object, which is too costly or too dangerous, or which is impossible to obtain. The mock-up may emphasize or highlight elements or components for learning and eliminate nonessential elements. Cut-aways, another type of model, are built in sections and can be taken apart to reveal the internal structure.

notes.front: What danger does the handbook see in test preparation material?
notes.back: Learners may pass a given test yet fail to learn other critical information essential to safe piloting and maintenance.
notes.explanation: Examiners report applicants who easily passed the knowledge test yet show a lack of knowledge under oral questioning.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Test Preparation Material”, p. 5-28
notes.evidence: the danger is that learners may be able to pass a given test, but fail to learn other critical information essential to safe piloting and maintenance practices. FAA inspectors and designated examiners report that learner applicants sometimes exhibit a lack of knowledge during oral questioning, even though many have easily passed the FAA knowledge test.

notes.front: How should blocks of learning be sized, and what should they represent?
notes.back: Fairly consistent in scope, representing units of learning that can be measured and evaluated, not a sequence of periods of instruction.
notes.explanation: Measurable blocks are combined progressively with related segments until their sum meets the overall training objectives.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Blocks of Learning”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: progressively combine these with other related segments until their sum meets the overall training objectives. The blocks of learning identified during the planning and management of a training activity should be fairly consistent in scope. They should represent units of learning which can be measured and evaluated—not a sequence of periods of instruction.

notes.front: A school adds three flights of aerobatics to its private pilot presolo stage "because learners enjoy them". What does the handbook say about blocks like these?
notes.back: C) Extraneous blocks are expensive frills that detract from, rather than assist in, completing the final objective
notes.explanation: The instructor should examine each block to ensure it is an integral part of the structure.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Blocks of Learning”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: During the process of identifying the blocks of learning to be assembled for the proposed training activity, the instructor should also examine each block to ensure it is an integral part of the structure. Extraneous blocks of instruction are expensive frills, especially in-flight instruction, and detract from, rather than assist in, the completion of the final objective.
notes.choices:
A) They are fine, since any extra flying builds skill
B) They are fine as long as they appear in the syllabus
C) Extraneous blocks are expensive frills that detract from, rather than assist in, completing the final objective
D) They are required to give learners a confidence boost
notes.choicesExplained: A: each block should be an integral part of the structure; extras are frills. B: being in the syllabus does not make an extraneous block integral. D: confidence comes from completing the necessary blocks, not from extra ones.

notes.front: Training under part 61, a learner's radio work is still weak, and the next syllabus lesson is a busy towered-airport trip. What does the handbook allow?
notes.back: C) Alter the order of training to suit the learner's progress; the syllabus is primarily a guide
notes.explanation: Any practical syllabus needs to be flexible; under part 61 the order of training can and should be altered to suit the learner's progress.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “How to Use a Training Syllabus”, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: Any practical training syllabus needs to be flexible and should be used primarily as a guide. Under 14 CFR part 61, the order of training can and should be altered to suit the progress of the learner and the demands of special circumstances.
notes.choices:
A) Keep strictly to the syllabus order, whatever the learner's progress
B) Stop training until the syllabus is rewritten
C) Alter the order of training to suit the learner's progress; the syllabus is primarily a guide
D) Skip the towered-airport lesson altogether
notes.choicesExplained: A: under part 61 the order can and should be altered to suit the learner. B: a syllabus should be flexible enough to adapt without suspending training. D: the order may change, but the required training still has to be completed.

notes.front: At a certificated school, what does compliance with the FAA-approved syllabus decide?
notes.back: Graduation: compliance with the appropriate, approved syllabus is a condition for graduation from the course.
notes.explanation: At such schools the syllabus is a key part of the training course outline, and facilities, aircraft and instructors support the course it specifies.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “How to Use a Training Syllabus”, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: At certificated schools, the syllabus is a key part of the training course outline. The instructional facilities, airport, aircraft, and instructor personnel support the course of training specified in the syllabus. Compliance with the appropriate, approved syllabus is a condition for graduation from such courses.

notes.front: An experienced instructor says she keeps all her lesson plans in her head. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: C) A mental outline is not a lesson plan; it should be written so another instructor could conduct the same lesson
notes.explanation: Written out, a lesson plan can also be analysed for adequacy and completeness.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Lesson Plans”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: A mental outline of a lesson is not a lesson plan. A lesson plan should be put into writing. Another instructor should be able to take the lesson plan and know what to do in conducting the same period of instruction. Written out, the lesson plan can be analyzed for adequacy and completeness.
notes.choices:
A) That is acceptable for experienced instructors
B) That is acceptable for one-on-one flight lessons
C) A mental outline is not a lesson plan; it should be written so another instructor could conduct the same lesson
D) Written plans are needed only for the practical test
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook makes no exception for experience. B: plans may be simpler for one-on-one training, but they are still put into writing. D: lesson plans should be prepared for each training period.

notes.front: Whatever their format, what three things should all aviation lesson plans include?
notes.back: Objectives, content to support the objectives, and completion standards.
notes.explanation: Terminology varies: completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, or performance evaluation, among others.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Lesson Plan Formats”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: All should include objectives, content to support the objectives, and completion standards. Various authorities often divide the main headings into several subheadings; terminology, even for the main headings, varies extensively. For example, completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, performance evaluation, or some other related term.

notes.front: On the flight instructor practical test, the applicant gives a preflight lesson on a manoeuvre. May lesson plans prepared beforehand be used?
notes.back: Yes: previously developed lesson plans from the applicant's library may be used.
notes.explanation: The evaluator asks for the lesson as it would be taught to a student and decides the outcome of the Task before the flight portion.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A “Maneuver Lesson”, p. 26
notes.evidence: Note: The evaluator asks the applicant to present a preflight lesson on the selected maneuver as the lesson would be taught to a student and determines the outcome of this Task before the flight portion of the practical test. Previously developed lesson plans from the instructor applicant's library may be used.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should assure a wise selection of material and {{c1::the elimination of unimportant details}}.
notes.back: the elimination of unimportant details
notes.explanation: Material is chosen deliberately, and what does not serve the lesson is left out.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Assure a wise selection of material and the elimination of unimportant details.

notes.front: An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should make certain that {{c1::due consideration is given to each part of the lesson}}.
notes.back: due consideration is given to each part of the lesson
notes.explanation: No part of the lesson is skimped because another part ran long.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Make certain that due consideration is given to each part of the lesson.

notes.front: An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should aid the instructor in presenting the material in {{c1::a suitable sequence for efficient learning}}.
notes.back: a suitable sequence for efficient learning
notes.explanation: The order of material is decided in advance with efficient learning in mind.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Aid the instructor in presenting the material in a suitable sequence for efficient learning.

notes.front: An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should provide {{c1::an outline of the teaching procedure}} to be used.
notes.back: an outline of the teaching procedure
notes.explanation: The plan sets out how the material will be taught, not only what.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Provide an outline of the teaching procedure to be used.

notes.front: An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should serve as a means of relating the lesson to {{c1::the objectives of the course of training}}.
notes.back: the objectives of the course of training
notes.explanation: Each lesson is tied back to what the whole course is trying to achieve.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Serve as a means of relating the lesson to the objectives of the course of training.

notes.front: A newly certificated instructor is nervous about her first ground lesson and writes a full lesson plan the night before. Which purpose of an adequate lesson plan speaks most directly to her situation?
notes.back: D) Giving the inexperienced instructor confidence
notes.explanation: One stated purpose of an adequate lesson plan, properly used, is to give the inexperienced instructor confidence.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Give the inexperienced instructor confidence.
notes.choices:
A) Promoting uniformity of instruction whatever the instructor or date
B) Eliminating unimportant details from the material
C) Relating the lesson to the objectives of the course of training
D) Giving the inexperienced instructor confidence
notes.choicesExplained: A: that serves learners who change instructor or day, not her nerves. C: that ties the lesson to the course, which is not her worry here. B: that concerns the selection of material, not the instructor's confidence.

notes.front: An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should promote {{c1::uniformity of instruction}} regardless of the instructor or the date on which the lesson is given.
notes.back: uniformity of instruction
notes.explanation: A learner who changes instructor, or flies on another day, gets the same lesson.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Purpose of the Lesson Plan”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Promote uniformity of instruction regardless of the instructor or the date on which the lesson is given.

notes.front: A lesson on engine failure after take-off also slips in unrelated material on radio licensing "because there was time". Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson is missing?
notes.back: D) Unity
notes.explanation: Unity means each lesson is a unified segment with limited objectives, and all procedures and materials are selected to attain them.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Unity—each lesson should be a unified segment of instruction. A lesson is concerned with certain limited objectives, which are stated in terms of desired learning outcomes. All teaching procedures and materials should be selected to attain these objectives.
notes.choices:
A) Scope
B) Practicality
C) Flexibility
D) Unity
notes.choicesExplained: A: the problem is not the amount of material but material unrelated to the lesson's objectives. B: practicality concerns the conditions under which the lesson is taught. C: flexibility is room for add-on material that serves the lesson, not unrelated topics.

notes.front: Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson requires new material that is related to the previous lesson?
notes.back: Content.
notes.explanation: A short review of earlier lessons is usually necessary, particularly in flight training.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Content—each lesson should contain new material. However, the new facts, principles, procedures, or skills should be related to the lesson previously presented. A short review of earlier lessons is usually necessary, particularly in-flight training.

notes.front: For a learner's first lesson on the subject, an instructor plans stalls, spins, steep turns and emergency descents in one flight. Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson is at risk?
notes.back: A) Scope
notes.explanation: A person can master only a few principles or skills at a time; too much material in a lesson results in confusion.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Scope—each lesson should be reasonable in scope. A person can master only a few principles or skills at a time, the number depending on complexity. Presenting too much material in a lesson results in confusion; presenting too little material results in inefficiency.
notes.choices:
A) Scope
B) Unity
C) Content
D) Relation to course of training
notes.choicesExplained: B: all four manoeuvres could serve one objective; the problem is how many there are. C: the lesson does contain new material; the issue is its amount. D: each manoeuvre can relate to the course; the issue is the load in one lesson.

notes.front: Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson means a plan for the aeroplane or ground trainer will differ from one for the classroom?
notes.back: Practicality: each lesson is planned in terms of the conditions under which the training is conducted.
notes.explanation: The kinds and quantities of instructional aids available also have a great influence on lesson planning.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Practicality—each lesson should be planned in terms of the conditions under which the training is to be conducted. Lesson plans conducted in an airplane or ground trainer will differ from those conducted in a classroom. Also, the kinds and quantities of instructional aids available have a great influence on lesson planning and instructional procedures.

notes.front: For flexibility, the outline of content in a lesson plan may include {{c1::blank spaces for add-on material}}, if required.
notes.back: blank spaces for add-on material
notes.explanation: The plan gives an outline and sequence, but a degree of flexibility should still be built in.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Flexibility—although the lesson plan provides an outline and sequence for the training to be conducted, a degree of flexibility should be incorporated. For example, the outline of content may include blank spaces for add-on material, if required.

notes.front: Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson requires each lesson's link to the course objectives to be clear to every learner?
notes.back: Relation to course of training.
notes.explanation: A lesson on short-field take-offs and landings, for example, should be related to both the certification and the safety objectives of the course.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: Relation to course of training—each lesson should be planned and taught so that its relation to the course objectives is clear to each learner. For example, a lesson on short-field takeoffs and landings should be related to both the certification and safety objectives of the course of training.

notes.front: Chapter 5 of the handbook names the four teaching-process steps preparation, presentation, application and assessment. How does chapter 7's 'instructional steps' characteristic name the fourth?
notes.back: Review and evaluation.
notes.explanation: Chapter 7 says every adequately developed lesson falls logically into these four steps; only the name of the last one differs.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Characteristics of a Well-Planned Lesson”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: Instructional steps—every lesson, when adequately developed, falls logically into the four steps of the teaching process: preparation, presentation, application, and review and evaluation.

notes.front: In pre-scenario planning for a flight scenario, instructor and learner establish the destination(s), desired learning outcomes, desired level of learner performance and {{c1::possible inflight scenario changes}}.
notes.back: possible inflight scenario changes
notes.explanation: The handbook calls establishing this information vital if SBT instruction is to be effective.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 7, “Pre-Scenario Planning”, p. 7-11
notes.evidence: For SBT instruction to be effective, it is vital that the aviation instructor and learner establish the following information: Flight scenario: ⦁ Scenario destination(s) ⦁ Desired learning outcomes ⦁ Desired level of learner performance ⦁ Possible inflight scenario changes
